items.prompt: What does BLUF stand for?
choices: Background laid out first
Bottom line up front
Brief, logical, unified format
items.explanation: BLUF means the bottom line comes first: the conclusion or request, before the supporting story.

items.prompt: In a BLUF message, what comes first?
choices: The conclusion or request
The history behind the topic
A greeting and a thank-you
items.explanation: The whole point of BLUF is to open with what the reader most needs: the conclusion or the request.

items.prompt: In a narrative-first message, what usually comes last?
choices: The background and the history
The sign-off and the writer's name
The actual request or conclusion
items.explanation: Narrative order follows the story of how things happened, so the point arrives at the end.

items.prompt: Which opening is a BLUF opening?
choices: "Let me begin with how this washer was bought, three years ago."
"Please keep the washer off until Thursday; the plumber needs it."
"There have been some thoughts about laundry around here lately."
items.explanation: Only the first opening states the request immediately. The others start with background or vague framing.

items.prompt: BLUF is mainly a change in what?
choices: The order of the information
The total length of the text
The friendliness of the tone
items.explanation: The same content can be written either way. BLUF only changes which part comes first.

items.prompt: Where did the BLUF habit come from?
choices: Newspaper crossword clues
Classroom essay rules
Military briefings
items.explanation: It began as a briefing convention for readers who needed the decision first, and spread to other writing.

items.prompt: Why does narrative order mirror the writer more than the reader?
choices: It follows how the reader will make the decision
It follows how the writer found the answer
It follows what the reader asked for first
items.explanation: Writers reconstruct their own path to the answer. The reader needs the answer, then the path if they want it.

items.prompt: If a reader can stop at any point, what does BLUF guarantee they have already seen?
choices: The most important part
Every supporting detail once
The full background story
items.explanation: Because the conclusion is first, stopping early never costs the reader the key point.

items.prompt: Note A spends three paragraphs on the washer's history and then says "please don't run it tonight." Note B says "please don't run it tonight" first, then gives the same history. What differs between them?
choices: Note B is shorter, so it is much clearer
Only the order; the information is identical
Note B hides the history from its readers
Note A is more polite, so it works better
items.explanation: Both notes contain the same facts. BLUF changes what a reader who stops early has already seen, not what the note says.
items.reference:
Same words, two orders
📜 Narrative-first — history, reasoning, then the request
📍 BLUF — the request and conclusion, then the reasoning
Same facts in both; only the order differs
Why: BLUF is a change of order, not of content: the conclusion comes first so a reader who stops early still has it.
items.learnMore:
Why BLUF exists

Writers tend to tell things in the order they discovered them. Readers need them in the order that lets them act. BLUF (bottom line up front) swaps one for the other.

Common mistake

Treating BLUF as a style of being brief. It is about where the conclusion sits, not how long the text is.
items.reflection: Think of the last long message you received. Where was the actual point, and how far did you read before finding it?

items.prompt: Which of these messages is NOT written BLUF-style, even though it is short?
choices: "The printer jammed twice, we tried two fixes, so: may I order a new one?"
"May I order a new printer? It jammed twice, and two fixes failed to help."
"Please approve a new printer for us, because the old one has jammed twice."
"Request: a new printer. Reason: two jams, and two fixes that failed."
items.explanation: Short does not mean BLUF. The first message still ends with the request, so a reader who stops early never sees it.

📜 Narrative-first — history, reasoning, then the request
📍 BLUF — the request and conclusion, then the reasoning
Same facts in both; only the order differs
Why: BLUF is a change of order, not of content: the conclusion comes first so a reader who stops early still has it.

items.prompt: Why do writers default to narrative order?
choices: Readers have asked for the story before the request
Putting the request first is generally considered rude
Context has to be given before a request is valid
It replays the order in which they found things out
items.explanation: Narrative order is the writer's own memory of events. Nothing about the reader's needs requires it, and a request is valid without a preamble.

items.prompt: What is "the ask" in a document?
choices: The background that explains the whole situation
The list of risks the writer can currently see
The decision or action wanted from the reader
items.explanation: The ask is what you want the reader to do or decide. It is stated, not left to be inferred.

items.prompt: What is a "stake"?
choices: How many people will end up reading the whole note
What changes if the reader says yes, no, or waits
The deadline printed on the cover page of the note
items.explanation: Stakes tell the reader what is riding on the decision, including the cost of doing nothing.

items.prompt: What is a "recommendation"?
choices: The path the writer thinks should be chosen
A summary of every option that was ever raised
The reader's own final answer to the ask
items.explanation: It is the writer's proposed choice, stated briefly before the full proof.

items.prompt: Where does supporting detail go?
choices: Before the ask, to earn the reader's trust
Instead of the ask when the note is short
After the ask, for whoever wants it
items.explanation: Detail is available but does not stand between the reader and the ask.

items.prompt: What does "self-contained" mean for an executive summary?
choices: It repeats the whole document word for word
A reader of only this part knows the request
It lists facts but makes no request at all
items.explanation: A self-contained summary can be read alone and still lets the reader act.

items.prompt: In this unit, who is the "executive"?
choices: Whoever can approve, reject, or redirect it
Anyone with a senior-sounding job title
Whoever knows the most about the topic
items.explanation: The word points to decision pressure, not seniority or expertise.

items.prompt: Which sentence states an ask rather than hinting at one?
choices: "The printer has been unreliable lately, sadly."
"Printers are a common problem in offices."
"Please approve the new printer by Friday."
items.explanation: Only the first one names a concrete action for the reader. The others just describe the situation.

items.prompt: In an inverted pyramid, each paragraph is...
choices: More detailed than the one before it was
Less essential than the one before it
Equally essential as all the others are
items.explanation: That ordering lets the reader stop anywhere and still hold the most important information.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a stake, rather than an ask, a recommendation, or background?
choices: "Please approve the replacement by March 1, if possible."
"I suggest buying the model the library already uses."
"If we wait past March, the warranty lapses."
"The printer was bought about four years ago, secondhand."
items.explanation: A stake describes what changes depending on the decision. The other three are the ask, the recommendation, and background.
items.reference:
The parts of a first block
🎯 The ask — the decision or action wanted
⚖️ The stake — what changes if yes, no, or wait
💡 The recommendation — the path you favor
📚 Supporting detail — evidence, placed after
Why: Name each part separately so the reader never has to infer what you want from them.
items.learnMore:
The vocabulary of a summary

An executive summary is only useful if a reader of that part alone knows what is wanted. The ask, the stake and the recommendation are three different things, and mixing them up produces summaries that describe a topic without requesting anything.

Common mistake

Writing a summary that describes the subject ("this note covers the printer") instead of stating what you want decided.
items.reflection: Pick any request you made recently. Can you state its ask, its stake and your recommendation as three separate sentences?

items.prompt: A summary says: "We should probably look into the printer situation at some point." What is missing?
choices: More history about how the printer was bought
A specific ask the reader could approve or decline
A longer list of supporting evidence for it
A friendlier greeting at the very top
items.explanation: The sentence names no decision, no deadline and no action. Without an ask, the reader has nothing to say yes or no to.

items.prompt: Which item does a self-contained summary NOT need to include?
choices: The full list of rejected alternatives
The decision that is being requested
The reason the decision matters right now
The path that the writer recommends most
items.explanation: Rejected alternatives are supporting detail. The ask, the reason now and the recommendation must be readable on their own.

items.prompt: What does BLUF cost a careful reader with plenty of time?
choices: Nothing; they still read all of it
Half of the detail they would otherwise get
The ability to follow the reasoning
items.explanation: They get the same content in a different order, so nothing is lost.

items.prompt: Which reader does narrative order fail?
choices: One who reads every single word slowly
One who already knows the background well
One who runs out of time before the point
items.explanation: If attention or time runs out first, the reader never reaches the ask.

items.prompt: A reader squeezes your note in between two meetings. What is likely?
choices: They will read it all the way to the end
They may stop at any moment
They will read only the final lines first
items.explanation: Interrupted readers cannot be counted on to reach the end.

items.prompt: Which order has no matching failure mode?
choices: Ask first, detail after
Context first, ask last
Ask buried in the middle
items.explanation: Putting the ask first never prevents the reader from also reading the rest.

items.prompt: You cannot tell how much time the reader will have. What follows?
choices: Use narrative order as the default
Ask the reader how long they have
Use BLUF as the default
items.explanation: Since BLUF is safe for both kinds of reader, it is the safer default.

items.prompt: In the flowchart, where does the narrative path lose the reader?
choices: When the reader disagrees with the ask
When time or attention runs out before the ask
When the reader forwards the document
items.explanation: The failure is positional: the ask sits after the point where the reader stopped.

items.prompt: Does BLUF remove any content from the document?
choices: No; it moves detail after the ask
Yes; it cuts the background entirely
Yes; it cuts the reasoning
items.explanation: Everything is still there. Only the order changes.

items.prompt: What does an unhurried reader experience under BLUF?
choices: Less information than before, overall
A document that is much harder to follow
The same information, in a different order
items.explanation: They lose nothing and arguably gain a clear frame for reading the rest.

items.prompt: A colleague says: "Our readers have lots of time, so the order of our documents doesn't matter." What is the best reply?
choices: Correct: with unlimited time, narrative order is strictly better
Wrong: unhurried readers cannot follow a narrative order at all
Wrong: BLUF always makes documents shorter, which saves them time
Perhaps, but BLUF costs them nothing and covers busier days
items.explanation: The argument is about asymmetry: BLUF has no downside for the careful reader and a clear upside for the interrupted one.
items.reference:
Two readers, two orders
🕒 Unhurried reader — reads all of it either way, loses nothing
⏱️ Interrupted reader — only BLUF puts the ask in front of them
❓ Unknown reader — you cannot tell in advance which one you have
Why: BLUF never costs the careful reader anything and protects the one who runs out of time.
items.learnMore:
The asymmetry

Narrative order has a failure mode, which is the reader who stops before the point. BLUF has no matching failure mode, because reading the ask first never prevents reading the detail afterwards.

Common mistake

Assuming BLUF is only for rushed readers. You usually cannot know in advance whether a reader will be rushed.
items.reflection: Where in your own life do you read in short gaps? What would you want the first line of anything sent to you to contain?

items.prompt: You are leaving a note for a neighbor whose schedule you do not know. Which opening minimizes the worst case?
choices: Start with the story of how the problem began
Put the request in the middle after some context
State the request and the reason first
Open with thanks and leave the request for the end
items.explanation: The worst case is a reader who stops early. Only an opening that carries the request protects against it.

items.prompt: A request was accurate, well reasoned, and ignored. Which explanation best fits the asymmetry argument?
choices: The reasoning was too brief to persuade anyone
The reader stopped before reaching the ask
The reader disagreed with the starting premises
The ask was too ambitious to be considered
items.explanation: Soundness does not guarantee attention. A well-argued ask that sits past the stopping point is never seen.

items.prompt: Which order does the inverted pyramid use?
choices: Background, detail, recommendation, why now, ask
Ask, why now, recommendation, detail, background
Why now, background, ask, detail, recommendation
items.explanation: Most essential first, least essential last.

items.prompt: Where does the history go in a BLUF document?
choices: Last, for whoever wants it
It is deleted from the document
First, to set the context
items.explanation: History is kept but demoted so it no longer stands between the reader and the ask.

items.prompt: Each section is progressively...
choices: More essential to a reader who stops there
Longer than the section before it
Less essential to a reader who stops there
items.explanation: The pyramid narrows from essential to optional.

items.prompt: The inverted pyramid was borrowed from which field?
choices: Architecture
Journalism
Accounting
items.explanation: Newspapers put the most important facts first because readers may stop at any paragraph.

items.prompt: What comes right after the ask?
choices: Why now: the stakes
The background history
The alternatives considered
items.explanation: Once the reader knows the ask, the next thing they need is why it matters now.

items.prompt: What happens to the background in the BLUF rewrite?
choices: It is removed to save space
It stays in the first position
It moves down to the last position
items.explanation: Nothing is thrown away; the background is simply demoted.

items.prompt: If a reader stops after the first section, they should...
choices: Know the full history of the issue
Know what is being asked of them
Know every alternative considered
items.explanation: The first section exists so an early stop still leaves the reader informed.

items.prompt: What is the third element in the pyramid?
choices: The recommendation
The background story
The thanks and sign-off
items.explanation: Ask, then stakes, then the recommended path.

items.prompt: A note about the washer has five pieces: (1) the washer's history, (2) the request not to run it before Thursday evening, (3) why: the plumber needs the water off, (4) a suggestion to use the laundromat this week, (5) which valve and which hours. Which order follows the inverted pyramid?
items.explanation: Request, stakes, recommendation, details, then history last. Chronological order (1 to 5) is the narrative order the pyramid replaces.
items.reference:
Most to least important
1️⃣ The ask
2️⃣ Why now (the stakes)
3️⃣ The recommendation
4️⃣ Supporting detail
5️⃣ Background
Why: Order by what a reader who stops here most needs, not by the order you learned things.
items.learnMore:
Ordering by importance

Each section should matter less to the decision than the one before. History and context are not discarded; they move to the end for whoever wants them.

Common mistake

Placing a section high because it took a lot of work to produce. Effort is not importance to the reader's decision.
items.reflection: Think of a report you wrote or read. If you reordered it purely by importance to the decision, what would move?

items.prompt: Which design choice breaks the inverted pyramid?
choices: Putting alternatives considered after the recommendation
Putting the deadline inside the ask itself
Putting the history in the final section
Putting a rich background section ahead of the stakes
items.explanation: Background is the least essential section, so placing it before the stakes inverts the intended order.

items.prompt: A section took days of research and is fascinating. Where should it go?
choices: Near the top, because effort deserves visibility
Nowhere; interesting material only distracts readers
Where its importance to the decision ranks, likely in the detail
In the opening, so readers will trust the rest
items.explanation: Position follows importance to the reader's decision, not effort or novelty.

items.prompt: Which set lists the four questions a working summary answers?
choices: Who wrote it, when, where filed, how long
History, reasoning, evidence, and thanks
Decision needed, why now, recommendation, cost
items.explanation: Those four give the reader enough to evaluate the ask.

items.prompt: What does "why now" answer?
choices: When the document was written
The specific cost of waiting
Who first noticed the problem
items.explanation: A good "why now" names the concrete consequence of delay.

items.prompt: What does the cost line show the reader?
choices: What they trade off by saying yes
How hard the writer has worked on it
Which team is to blame for it
items.explanation: It makes the trade-off visible so the reader can weigh it.

items.prompt: Advocacy shows...
choices: Both the upside and the trade-off
Only the risks
Only the upside
items.explanation: Analysis shows both sides. Advocacy sells only the favorable half.

items.prompt: Which ask is too vague to approve?
choices: "Approve this by Friday morning."
"We should look at this eventually."
"Choose option A or option B today."
items.explanation: A vague ask gives the reader nothing concrete to accept or decline.

items.prompt: Does leaving out the cost make it disappear?
choices: No; the reader finds it later
Yes, unless the reader asks
Yes, if the document is short
items.explanation: The trade-off exists whether or not it is written. Hiding it costs trust.

items.prompt: Why put a deadline inside the ask?
choices: It makes the document look longer
It replaces the recommendation
The reader knows by when to decide
items.explanation: A date turns a vague wish into a decision with a clock.

items.prompt: How should the recommendation appear in the summary?
choices: In full, with no short version anywhere
Briefly, with the proof coming after
Left out until the reader asks
items.explanation: The summary states the path; the detail follows below for those who want it.

items.prompt: Which first block answers all four questions?
choices: "The current printer has failed twice and the warranty ends in March. I suggest the model the library uses. It costs more than repairs and uses the chair budget."

"Please approve a replacement printer by March 1. The current one has failed twice and the warranty ends in March. I suggest the model the library uses. It costs more than repairs and uses the chair budget."
"Please approve a replacement printer by March 1. The current one has failed twice and the warranty ends in March. I suggest the model the library uses."
"Please approve a replacement printer by March 1. I suggest the model the library uses. It costs more than repairs and uses the chair budget."
items.explanation: Each wrong block drops one question: no ask, no cost, or no reason to act now. Only the first has all four.
items.reference:
The first block answers four things
❓ What decision, by when?
⏳ Why now? the cost of waiting
💡 What do you recommend?
⚖️ What does it cost? the trade-off
Why: Without the cost, a summary reads as advocacy; with it, as analysis the reader can trust.
items.learnMore:
What the first few lines hold

A reader deciding whether to keep reading needs enough to evaluate the ask, not just notice it. Four questions provide that, and the cost line is the one writers most often drop.

Common mistake

Dropping the cost to make approval likelier. The trade-off does not vanish; the reader finds it later, at a worse moment.
items.reflection: Next time you want something from someone, write the cost of saying yes in one sentence. Does the request feel different?

items.prompt: The writer drops the cost line to make approval easier. What is the most likely result?
choices: Trust drops when the reader finds the cost later
Approval is faster and nothing else changes
The reader assumes the cost must be small
The ask becomes clearer because it is shorter
items.explanation: Hidden costs are usually found. Once found, the reader doubts everything else in the summary.

"Many other teams have faced a very similar problem."
"We have been thinking about this for a long time now."
"The vendor's price rises May 1, and the old contract cannot be renewed."
items.explanation: A strong "why now" is specific and tied to a date or consequence. The others are vague or only gesture at importance.

"Let me know your thoughts on printers whenever it is convenient for you."
"Approve spending on a replacement printer by Friday, before exams."
"Think about printer options sometime before the term ends this year."
items.explanation: The first names an action, a deadline and a reason. The others invite a vague reaction instead of a decision.

items.prompt: Shortening a narrative draft leaves the ask...
choices: Still at the end
Now at the start
Removed entirely
items.explanation: Cutting words does not change where the ask sits.

items.prompt: What fixed Jordan's draft?
choices: Cutting the draft down to a single page
Adding more history at the very start
Moving the ask from the end to the start
items.explanation: Position was the problem, so changing the position was the fix.

items.prompt: In ninety seconds, which paragraph did the VP never reach?
choices: The first history paragraph
The one containing the ask
The team-capacity paragraph
items.explanation: The ask was the final paragraph, past the point where attention ran out.

items.prompt: Which facts does the rewrite keep?
choices: All of them, reordered
Only the recommended ones
None; it is fully new
items.explanation: The rewrite keeps every fact and changes only the order.

items.prompt: How is the old history labeled in the rewrite?
choices: Appendix, deleted before it is sent
Executive summary for the reader
Background, for whoever is still reading
items.explanation: It stays available but is clearly marked as optional.

items.prompt: Why can a well-reasoned ask still fail?
choices: Executives dislike reasoning of any kind
Good reasoning does not decide if it is read
Reasoning belongs only in conversation
items.explanation: A strong argument no one reaches persuades no one.

items.prompt: Which fix addresses an ask that comes last?
choices: Reordering
Trimming
Neither of them
items.explanation: Only reordering changes where the ask sits.

items.prompt: What can a stopped reader do after the rewrite's opening block?
choices: Learn the full history
Read the appendix
Make a decision
items.explanation: The opening block carries the ask, stakes, recommendation and cost.

items.prompt: Draft A is a ten-paragraph narrative. Draft B is the same story cut to three paragraphs, in the same order. A reader stops after thirty seconds. Which is true?
choices: B is safe, because shorter documents get read fully
Neither is safe; both still put the ask last
A is safer, because more detail persuades better
B is safe, because three paragraphs fit in thirty seconds
items.explanation: Shorter only moves the cutoff point. The ask remains the final item in both drafts.
items.reference:
Trimming vs. reordering
✂️ Trim — shorter, ask still last
🔀 Reorder — ask moves to the first line
The failure was position, not length
Why: Cutting words reduces the cost of reaching the ask; only moving the ask removes the problem.
items.learnMore:
Why shorter is not the fix

A shortened narrative draft still buries the ask. Jordan's ask was well justified and also the one sentence the reader never reached.

Common mistake

Fixing length when the actual defect is position.
items.reflection: Recall a document you tried to improve by cutting it down. Did the main point move, or only the amount of text around it?

items.prompt: Which edit to the original draft fixes the failure with the least change?
choices: Move the request into an opening block
Delete the first paragraph of history
Bold the request where it sits at the end
Add a table of contents above the draft
items.explanation: Bolding and a contents list help scanning but the reader still has to reach or find the request. Moving it guarantees it is seen.

items.prompt: The narrative draft needs about 148 words of reading before the ask; the BLUF opening needs about 79. At 400 words per minute, what is the most accurate reading?
choices: About 22 seconds versus 12; the gap no longer matters
About 44 seconds versus 24; speed does not change them
About 12 seconds for both; fast readers skip the setup
About 22 seconds versus 12; BLUF is still about half
items.explanation: Time is words divided by speed: 148/400 minutes is about 22 seconds and 79/400 minutes is about 12 seconds. Both halve, and the ratio stays near one half.

items.prompt: Does BLUF apply only to proposals?
choices: Yes, it only applies to proposals
No; any document a reader may stop early
Yes, it only applies to emails
items.explanation: The principle covers any document where the reader might stop at any point.

items.prompt: What leads a status update?
choices: Current status and impact
The project's full history
A request for approval
items.explanation: A stopped reader most needs where things stand and what it affects.

items.prompt: A short report on an incident leads with...
choices: A detailed timeline of the whole week
Thanks to everyone who was involved
What broke, the state now, and the response
items.explanation: The reader needs the situation and the response first.

items.prompt: What is the general principle behind BLUF?
choices: Always use the same four questions, in order
Lead with what matters most to a stopped reader
Always lead with the recommendation first
items.explanation: The four questions are one application of the principle, not the principle.

items.prompt: Is the four-question block universal?
choices: No; it fits requests for a decision
Yes, it fits every kind of document
Only for reports that run long
items.explanation: Other documents front-load other information.

items.prompt: A note that needs no decision should...
choices: Skip the opening and start with details
Invent an ask for approval
Still lead with the key news
items.explanation: Even an informational note benefits from a clear first line.

items.prompt: Why does one template for every document fail?
choices: Templates are banned in most places
Documents front-load different information
Readers dislike any visible structure
items.explanation: The principle is general; the specific contents of the opening are not.

items.prompt: What is the worked example in this unit?
choices: One case, not the whole territory
The complete rulebook for every document
A mandatory template to copy
items.explanation: It illustrates the principle on one document. Other documents need their own opening.

items.prompt: A document reports that a project is two weeks behind and needs no decision. Which opening is best?
choices: "A history of the project and the team changes since January, followed by the delay."
"Request: please approve an extra helper for the project, starting next week."
"The project is two weeks behind; no customer impact yet; the new estimate is June 12."
"Thank you for your support on this effort; details on the schedule follow below."
items.explanation: A status update leads with status, impact and the next estimate. The others bury the news, invent a request, or open with thanks.
items.reference:
Same principle, different opening
📝 Decision request — ask, why now, recommendation, cost
📊 Status update — status, impact, change, next estimate
🚨 Incident summary — what broke, current state, what is being done
Why: Lead with what matters most to a reader who stops; what that is depends on the document.
items.learnMore:
What carries over, what does not

The principle (lead with what matters most to a stopped reader) is general. The specific four questions fit a request for a decision. An update or a report needs a different opening.

Common mistake

Using one template for every document and forcing a request shape onto documents that ask for nothing.
items.reflection: Choose a document you write regularly that asks for nothing. What would a stopped reader most need in its first two lines?

items.prompt: The heating failed overnight in one building. Which first sentence best serves a reader who stops after it?
choices: "At around two in the morning, the first sensor reported a temperature drop in the east building."
"Heating failed overnight in the east building; it works again; a lasting fix is set for Friday."
"We are sorry for any inconvenience caused by the heating issue earlier this week, to everyone."
"Request: please approve a larger maintenance budget for next year, for the whole site."
items.explanation: The best opening states what happened, where things stand now, and what happens next. A timeline, an apology or an unrelated request leaves the reader less informed.

items.prompt: A team adopts one four-question template for all its documents. What goes wrong?
choices: Documents that need no decision get forced into a request
Readers can no longer stop reading early at all
Every document grows longer than the last one did
The ask moves to the end of each document
items.explanation: The template fits requests for a decision. Applied to updates or reports, it forces an artificial request.
